Abstract 50

Hydrated carbonates uniquely record low-temperature interactions between CO₂-rich 51

fluids and crustal rocks in water-rich conditions. Hydrated carbonates had not been 52

previously detected in situ on the surface of Mars, but the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover 53

reveals a local ~3.7-billion-year-old sediment preserving grains of hydrated Mg- 54

carbonate only ~1 cm below the surface. This sediment, located at the ancient lake 55

margin of Jezero Crater, was analyzed by the Scanning Habitable Environments with 56

Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals (SHERLOC) instrument aboard 57

Perseverance. The hydrated magnesium carbonate, spatially associated with amorphous 58

silica, formed through olivine alteration by aqueous CO₂ – a process known as mineral 59

carbonation – indicating early-stage alteration in an alkaline, water-rich environment. 60

This carbonate is closely associated with hydrous and anhydrous sulfates, anhydrous 61

carbonates, phosphate, and perchlorate, reflecting formation in multiple, temporally 62

distinct aqueous environments. A very localized long-term preservation of this hydrated 63

carbonate indicates exceptional local boundary conditions at the bedrock, including 64

water-rich, alkaline chemistry and effective shallow-subsurface thermal and diagenetic 65

shielding over geologic timescales. Discovery of hydrated carbonate also offers new in 66

situ evidence of Mars’s long-missing CO2 sink. 67

Introduction 68

The Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater to investigate the planet’s ancient 69

habitability and collect samples for eventual return to Earth as part of NASA’s Mars 2020 70

mission (M2020 SDT, 1). Jezero was selected as a landing site due to its well-preserved 71

sedimentary delta fans, sourced from mature watersheds, and its widespread olivine- 72

carbonate assemblages – features that collectively suggest a warm and long-lived, water- 73

rich environment during late Noachian or early Hesperian (~3.6-3.8 Ga) (2). 74

Carbonates form when olivine reacts with aqueous CO₂, a process known as mineral 75 carbonation (3). Spectral data from orbit confirm olivine carbonation in several regions of 76 Mars, including the watershed of Jezero Crater (4), supporting the prediction of a surface 77 carbonate reservoir (5). Yet in situ confirmation of large carbonate deposits expected 78 from the sequestration of a once-thicker CO₂-rich atmosphere has been lacking (6) but is 79 now being uncovered by rover missions (7,8). Hydrated carbonates, however, had 80 previously only been inferred from orbit (9,10). 81

Since landing, Perseverance has explored and collected samples from a range of geologic 82

units through sequential science campaigns, including the crater floor, fan front, upper 83

fan, Margin unit, and crater rim (11,12). The crater Margin campaign (Fig. 1A), through 84


<!-- Page 6 -->


summer 2024, focused on the transitional zone between the western delta edge and the 85

crater rim. A recent study proposed that the Margin formed either through magmatic 86

intrusion or by lava overflowing the crater rim following impact (13). Orbital 87

interpretations confirm that the Margin unit predates western fan sediments and Neretva 88

Vallis River channel (Fig. 1A and B) (13,14). The observations made by instruments on 89

Perseverance indicate that rocks in the Margin unit experienced multiple temporally and 90

chemically discrete aqueous alteration events (13). Margin unit rocks consist of primary 91

igneous grains (olivine, pyroxene), a combination of detrital carbonate clasts, secondary 92

void-filling carbonate phases, alteration of primary igneous clasts to carbonate, and other 93

alteration phases such as serpentine-group minerals, hydrated silica, and sulfate (13). 94

We investigated the mineralogy and aqueous history of Jezero’s Margin unit rocks using 95

the SHERLOC instrument (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and 96

Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals) on the Perseverance rover (15). SHERLOC 97

is a deep-ultraviolet fluorescence and Raman spectrometer capable of detecting and 98

identifying organic compounds and minerals at spatial resolutions to 100 μm (15). 99

SHERLOC spectral data were complemented by elemental chemistry and mineral 100

identifications from Perseverance’s PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray 101

Lithochemistry) instrument (16). 102

We report a novel in situ detection of hydrated magnesium carbonate in the Amherst 103

Point abrasion target (sol 915) of the Hans Amundsen Memorial Workspace outcrop, 104

which is located at the easternmost exposure of the Margin unit, adjacent to the delta fan 105

(Fig. 1B). The detection and preservation of hydrated carbonate with sulfate, phosphate, 106

and perchlorate, reinforces a dynamic fluid-rock interaction history of Margin rocks and 107

potential hydrated niches in the shallow subsurface. Especially, the discovery expands the 108

surface inventory of carbonate phases on Mars, offering new evidence of Mars’s long- 109

missing CO₂ sink (6) that is now being uncovered. 110

Results 111

Textures and composition of Amherst Point 112

The first abrasion operation of the Jezero crater Margin unit, Amherst Point, was 113

conducted on sol 915 at the Hans Amundsen Memorial Workspace, located at the 114

easternmost exposure of the Margin unit (Fig. 1B). Outcrops in this region are 115

pervasively fractured into irregular polygons, with spheroidal weathering noted as 116

concentric fracturing along polygon edges (Fig. 1C). Polygons have a gentle, convex- 117

upward surface, and in cross-section display decimeter-scale planar bedding (Fig. 1C, 118

inset). Outcrop surfaces are typically dusty and show irregular mm-scale protrusions (Fig. 119

1D and E) consisting of multiple adjacent grains (Fig. 1E, inset). Detailed imaging of the 120

workspace (Fig. 1F) also reveals an erosion-resistant cross-cutting linear feature, which is 121

inferred to represent a mineralized vein formed through post-depositional fluid-rock 122


<!-- Page 7 -->


interaction (Fig. 1G). The rock exposed in the Amherst Point abrasion patch (~5 cm wide 123

and ~1 cm deep) is texturally and compositionally heterogeneous (Figs. 2A-C). Overall, 124

the rock lacks the interlocking texture of grains common to igneous rocks and is therefore 125

interpreted as a clastic sedimentary rock that reflects reworking of local igneous 126

lithologies (13). The abrasion surface exposes a variety of grain types, including angular, 127

rounded, and composite grains (mean size 0.65 mm, ± 0.16 mm, n=350), which would 128

suggest a moderately to poorly sorted, medium to coarse-grained sandstone (Figs. 2A-C). 129

The rock’s color also varies from brighter-toned to reddish-brown areas surrounding 130

darker grains (Figs. 2A-C). 131

Jezero Crater Margin contains hydrated magnesium carbonate 132

SHERLOC Raman spectroscopy on the Amherst Point abraded patch (Fig. 2D) was 133

acquired on sols 920 and 921. Deep UV Raman and fluorescence spectra were acquired 134

from two different scans that included 4 “detail” scans (1×1 mm, 100 points, 100 µm 135

spacing, 500 pulses per point) and 2 “survey” scans (5×5 mm, 1296 points, 144 µm 136

spacing, 15 pulses per point) (Figs. 2E and F). 137

On sol 921, SHERLOC acquired four spectra that showed scatter peaks characteristic of 138

hydrated carbonates, mostly associated with pale white material (Figs 3A-D). Three such 139

spectra were in detail scan 1 (points 68, 87, and 92), and one in detail scan 2 (point 95), 140

see ROIs in Figs. 3A and B. The v1 Raman peak for the spectra corresponding to points 141

68, 88, 92, and 95 was centered at 1102 (± 2.7), 1096 (± 2.0), 1096 (±1.9), and 1104 142

(±1.8) cm-1 respectively, with signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) values of ≥10 (Fig. 3E and 143

Table S1), with broad hump in the OH stretching region with a peak maximum of 3382 144

(±28.6), 3448 (±8.0), 3499 (±9.8), and 3310 (±22.3) respectively, with SNR values ≥8 145

(Table S1). 146

These spectra were compared with those of hydrated carbonate minerals in the lab, using 147

the SHERLOC analog instruments in flight mode configuration (Fig. 3) (15). SHERLOC 148

spectra of points 68, 87, 95 and 95 (with v1 peak position ranging from 1095 to 1104 cm-1 149

and hydration peak from 3310 to 3499 cm-1) are similar to laboratory spectra of 150

nesquehonite (MgCO3·3H2O) and lansfordite (MgCO3·5H2O) as shown in Fig. 3E and 151

Table S1, which are the low-temperature hydrated carbonate phases (17). However, the 152

Raman peak position of the hydrated carbonate varies among these eight SHERLOC 153

spectra by ~10 wavenumbers for the v1 mode and by more than 100 wavenumbers for the 154

OH stretching band. In addition, the determination of peak position contains error, and its 155

calculation is described in the methods section. Due to this uncertainty in SHERLOC peak 156

positions (or effects of Fe substitutions, see Fig. S1), this band assignment is not 157

definitive. It is more reasonable and cautious to assign these detections to a class of 158

minerals (18), namely the hydrous magnesium carbonates. Although it is conceivable from 159

*Fig. 3E that the detected hydrous magnesium carbonate phase or phases have not fully 160*

dehydrated to hydromagnesite (19). 161

Identification and deconvolution of hydrated carbonate associated with hydrated 162

sulfate 163

Four other SHERLOC spectra in detail 1 scan contained evidence of hydration; however, 164

spatially associated with both carbonate and sulfate in points 71, 88, 90, and 91 (see ROIs 165

on Figs. 3A and B, Table S1). The v1 Raman peak for hydrated carbonate associated with 166

points 71, 88, 90, and 91 was centered at 1092 (±1.9), 1095 (± 1.9), 1095 (±2.2), and 1092 167

(±1.8) cm-1 respectively, with SNR values of ≥14.6 (Table S1), and OH stretching region 168

peak maximum of 3475 (±13.9), 3377 (±5.2), 3442 (±7.2), and 3459 (±2.61) respectively, 169

with SNR values ≥7.6 (Table S1). Point 91, on the lightest-toned material analyzed, had 170

the strongest v1 scatter and hydration peaks, but also showed the v3 carbonate 171

antisymmetric stretching modes at 1427, 1517, and the H2O bending mode at 1670 cm-1. 172

These v3 antisymmetric mode peaks positions in point 91 are consistent with SHERLOC 173

analog spectra of the hydrated carbonate nesquehonite standard, suggesting the presence 174

of hydrated carbonate in point 91, alongside a low intensity hydrated sulfate peak (Fig. 175

S3). 176

In the regions of interest belonging to presumably hydrated sulfate (Fig. 3A), the v1 peak 177

is consistently positioned at 1023 cm-1 in all four points 71, 88, 90, and 91, with fitting 178

error values accounting for ±4.4, ±1.4, ±2, and ±0.8 cm-1, respectively (Fig. 3E and Table 179

S1). All points containing sulfate peaks exhibit an OH band signal, with their peaks 180

located between ~3442 and 3475 cm-1 (Fig. 3E and Table S1), similar to magnesium 181

sulfate trihydrate (Table S1), consistent with what has been observed in the Jezero crater 182

floor campaign (20). The peak positions for the OH stretching band in all eight hydration 183

points (Fig. 3A and B) do not seem to change as a function of the presence or absence of 184

hydrated sulfate, although they span a wide range between ~3310-3509 cm-1. 185

The intensities of OH bands are greater when sulfate is present than when sulfate is absent 186

(ROI in Fig. 4A), supporting that the sulfate is hydrated (Fig. 4B). Previous studies of 187

hydrated sulfates have shown that the intensity of the OH bands typically correlates well 188

with the intensity of the sulfate v1 band, indicating that hydration in these targets primarily 189

comes from sulfates (20,21) (Fig. S4). In Amherst Point, the intensity of the OH bands is 190

not correlated with the intensity of the sulfate v1 band, showing the OH band intensities 191

have contributions from both carbonates and sulfates (Fig. 4B). 192

The detection of pure hydrated carbonate phases rather than of anhydrous carbonate mixed 193

with hydrated sulfate is also clear in a linear relationship between the carbonate v1 peak 194

intensity and the area of the hydration band for points 68, 87, 92 (Fig. 4C), which have no 195

sulfate v1 peak, and both v1 carbonate and OH stretching band signals are strong (v1 SNR: 196

12, 43, 41, respectively) and (OH SNR: 8, 33, 12, respectively), see Fig. 3E and Table S1. 197

These observations support a carbonate phase as a likely hydration carrier in the sol 921 198

detail 1 scan and strengthen our inference that hydrated carbonate is detected in at least 199

three spectra in detail 1, as well as one spectrum in detail 2 (Figs. 3A-E). The average 200


<!-- Page 9 -->


spectra of points 68, 87, and 92 (Fig. 4D) further support the categorical detection of 201

hydrated carbonate in detail 1 scan. 202

Additionally, the points in Amherst Point with observed sulfate and hydration signatures 203

do not show a clear correlation between the hydration band area and sulfate peak intensity 204

(Fig. S4). This is in contrast to the linear correlation observed for the hydrated sulfates in 205

the Dourbes abrasion target of the crater floor unit, Seitah, for instance (20,21). This linear 206

relationship for Dourbes showed that the hydration feature can be attributed to sulfates and 207

that these sulfates have a consistent degree of hydration. The lack of correlation we 208

observe at Amherst Point thus shows that the hydration feature cannot be attributed solely 209

to sulfates. 210

PIXL correlation of hydrated carbonate 211

To constrain the chemistry and context of the hydrous carbonate materials, element 212

abundance maps from the PIXL instrument (16) were correlated with the SHERLOC 213

Raman spectra (Fig. S1). The SHERLOC Raman locations showing peaks from hydrous 214

carbonate (Figs. 3A-B) had PIXL element abundances consistent with significant 215

proportions of Fe- and Mg-carbonate, but not Ca-bearing carbonate (Fig. S1). This 216

interpretation is consistent with a relatively high MgO (≤22.7 wt%) and CO2 (≤29.4 wt%) 217

content in the areas where hydrated Mg-carbonate is located (Table S2). 218

To constrain the identity of the hydrous magnesium carbonate phase from PIXL chemical 219

data, the elemental/oxide relevant magnesium carbonate minerals were computed from 220

their stoichiometric endmember formulae (Table S3) and compared to chemical 221

compositions of PIXL analyses (PMC points) where hydrated Mg-carbonate was detected 222

(Table S2). The endmember compositions were used to determine MgO:CO2 wt.% ratios 223

from Raman data for comparison to PIXL data. The Raman spectra of points 71, 68, 90, 224

91, 92, and 95 give a mean MgO/CO2 weight ratio from 0.74 to 0.87 (Table S2, S3), 225

which could be consistent with the minerals nesquehonite, lansfordite, or magnesite. 226

Carbonate in points 87 and 88 could correspond to a mixture of anhydrous Mg- and Fe 227

carbonate and hydrated magnesium carbonate, given the MgO/CO2 ratio for these points 228

falls slightly below the threshold for pure nesquehonite, lansfordite, and endmember 229

magnesite, but their Raman spectra exhibit a strong hydration feature (Tables S2 and S3; 230

*Fig. 3-4). 231*

For each PIXL analysis volume, its maximum possible H₂O content (Table S2) was 232

estimated based on the deficit in analytical totals, where non-negative values indicate 233

potential hydration. While it is unclear if hydration arises from carbonate, sulfate, or 234

some unrecognized component(s), H₂O is the most plausible source in most cases given 235

the pervasive hydration feature observed in the SHERLOC scans (Fig. 3). Using known 236

H₂O content for hydrated carbonates (~19–52 wt.%), the average H2O values in Table S3 237

serve as upper limits to constrain the mole fractions of hydrated carbonate or sulfate 238

phases via mass balance. The heterogeneity in average H2O values in Table S3, observed 239


<!-- Page 10 -->


for all SHERLOC hydrated carbonate detection points, including points 87 and 88, 240

indicates that a hydration component may be heterogeneously distributed within the 241

SHERLOC analysis area, as shown in Figs. 3A-B. 242

Mineral contacts and zoning 243

Olivine was identified from its Raman scatter peaks near 811-830 cm-1 in the sol 921 244

detail scan (Fig. 3F). By the peak positions, it is not pure forsterite (Mg2SiO4) and is 245

inferred to contain significant Fe in solid solution (consistent with PIXL analyses) (see 246

Figs. 3F and S1). The sol 921 detail scans exhibited an anhydrous carbonate phase with v1 247

peak centered at ~1089-1093 cm-1 corresponding to siderite or magnesite (Fig. 3F) that are 248

spatially associated with hydrated Mg-carbonate (Fig. 3A and B). SHERLOC also 249

revealed anhydrous sulfate detections in a few points in sol 921 detail 1 (Fig. 3A and B), 250

positioned at ~1028 cm-1 (Figs. 3F and S1). Raman peaks at ~930-970 cm-1 were also 251

identified in the Amherst Point two-sol detail scans corresponding to perchlorate and 252

phosphate (Fig. 3F). 253

The PIXL phase maps of chemistry and mineralogy reflect the measurement (wt.%) and 254

distribution of major and minor mineral phases across the PIXL and SHERLOC detail 255

scan areas within the Amherst Point abrasion patch (Fig. 5). PIXL phase maps identify 256

olivine, carbonate, and silica (SiO₂) (Figs. 5A and B) spatially associated with hydrated 257

Mg-carbonate (Fig. 5B). Olivine and Mg/Fe carbonate dominate the abrasion patch and 258

are commonly in contact with Mg/Fe carbonate locally replacing olivine (Figs. 5A and B) 259

consistent with olivine carbonation. Especially, hydrated Mg-carbonate occurs 260

preferentially along olivine grain margins, with silica (SiO2) spatially associated with 261

hydrated Mg-carbonate in a cross-cutting vein (Fig. 5B). Both hydrated carbonate and 262

silica are the primary alteration products of olivine carbonation (22). This is also 263

consistent with PIXL-based alteration mapping of the Eastern Margin Unit (23). 264

Overall, SHERLOC and PIXL maps reveal a heterogeneous distribution of olivine, 265

hydrous and anhydrous Mg/Fe carbonate, silica, hydrous and anhydrous sulfate, phosphate 266

and perchlorate (Figs 3A-B and 5A-B), with PIXL maps showing a spatial zoning with 267

silica-rich cores rimmed by hydrated carbonate and hydrated sulfate (Fig. 5B-D). 268

Additionally, the spatial overlap between carbonate, sulfate, phosphate, and perchlorate 269

suggests sequential alteration, where carbonation was followed by sulfate precipitation 270

during later fluid infiltration events. 271

The locations of the SHERLOC Raman spectra were overlaid onto WATSON (Wide- 272

Angle Topographic Sensor for Operations and eNgineering) camera images to allow 273

correlation of spectra with rock textures. Olivine, sulfate, and carbonate phases are 274

spatially associated, with hydrated phases present within lighter-toned intergranular spaces 275

(Fig. 3B and D). Olivine, perchlorate, and/or phosphate, as well as hydrous and anhydrous 276

sulfate, and hydrous and anhydrous carbonate, spatially and spectrally co-occur in several 277

points, located in both darker and lighter-toned areas. However, there are points where 278

they occur independently. 279

Discussion 280

A carbonation-driven dynamic formation environment 281

The in situ detection of hydration in Martian carbonate phases is broadly consistent with 282

orbital infrared observations first reported in 1969 by the Mariner 6 and 7 flyby spacecraft, 283

which identified absorption features at 2.28 and 5.4 µm – diagnostic of hydrous Mg- 284

carbonate phases such as hydromagnesite (Mg₅(CO₃)₄(OH)₂·4H₂O) and artinite 285

(Mg₂(CO₃)(OH)₂·3H₂O) – primarily across the southern hemisphere (9). 286

Orbital near-infrared spectra of the Jezero region, particularly along the Margin unit near 287

Neretva Vallis, also reveal absorption bands consistent with hydrated Mg-carbonate, 288

suggesting an authigenic deposition of carbonates in a sustained aqueous environment 289

from the Noachian to early Hesperian (e.g., 8). Indeed, the orbital data are best explained 290

by hydrated Mg-carbonate (9,10), although alternative interpretations suggest the presence 291

of additional hydrated phases, such as smectite (24). By contrast, Perseverance’s in situ 292

analyses show that most Jezero carbonate phases are anhydrous and contain both Fe and 293

Mg carbonate, typically associated with olivine, hydrated Mg-sulfate and anhydrous Ca- 294

sulfate, and perchlorate, in both the crater floor and delta fan targets (21,25). This is 295

similar to the mineral assemblage observed at Amherst Point, although these targets 296

exhibit less abundant silica phases. Silica might have a stabilizing influence on hydrated 297

carbonate (26) in Amherst Point. This inconsistency suggests that orbital carbonate 298

detections (e.g., 10) may often reflect mixtures with hydrated silicate phases rather than 299

widespread hydrated carbonate, implying that pure hydrated carbonate phases are rare on 300

the Martian surface. Hydrated carbonate is not even detected in other Margin targets (13); 301

hence, it is the sole detection by any lander mission to Mars. 302

We propose that the hydrated carbonate formed through carbonation-driven precipitation, 303

with Mg/Fe carbonates replacing olivine at multiple locations in Amherst Point (Fig. 5A 304

and B). This suggests that the original olivine underwent aqueous carbonation, 305

accompanied by the formation of serpentine phases and amorphous silica (Fig. 5) (23). 306

Spatial patterns in PIXL data further document these replacement textures at sub- 307

millimeter scales, with carbonate–silicate associations (Figs. 5A and B) consistent with 308

progressive carbonation of olivine. 309

The formation of Jezero margin carbonates could include a combination of processes (10), 310

such as near-shore lacustrine carbonate precipitation and fluvial transport of detrital 311

materials, with the southern deposits most consistent with an authigenic lacustrine origin. 312

Their topographic restriction to the pre-breach shoreline elevations of Jezero Crater 313

indicates formation during an early, closed-basin phase of the paleolake, when high 314

alkalinity and shallow, Mg-rich waters favored carbonate deposition. While some 315

carbonate could have been added later or through detrital input, the mineralogy and spatial 316

trends suggest that the Marginal carbonates represent near-shore, fluvio-lacustrine 317

deposition before the outlet breach (10). 318


<!-- Page 12 -->


However, olivine carbonation provides the most plausible explanation for hydrated Mg- 319

carbonate formation, as supported by the mineralogical and geochemical evidence in Figs. 320

5A and B. It is noted that the composition of local fluid chemistry is not uniquely 321

constrained; therefore, precise replication of a localized parent fluid chemistry is not 322

possible. Our hypothesis of carbonation-driven hydrated carbonate precipitation is also 323

consistent with a new, broader Jezero Margin study of carbonated ultramafic rocks (13). 324

In a MgO–CO2–H2O system, the hydrated Mg carbonate intermediates will precipitate 325

first, because, although magnesite is thermodynamically favored, it is hindered by slow 326

kinetics (27). Mg2+ is highly soluble in water; as the Mg2+·6H2O complex (or magnesium 327

cation coordinated by six water molecules) has a high energy barrier for dehydration 328

(ΔhydG° = −1903.72 kJ mol−1) (28), the formation of hydrated Mg carbonates will precede 329

the formation of magnesite and dolomite (CaMg(CO₃)₂) (27). Direct precipitation of 330

magnesite typically requires elevated temperatures (>100°C), microbial mediation, or 331

recrystallization or dehydration of its hydrous precursors at ambient temperatures and 332

pressures (e.g., 29). An experimental heat treatment of hydrated Mg carbonates yielded a 333

transformation sequence, with increasing temperature, of: lansfordite → nesquehonite → 334

dypingite → hydromagnesite → magnesite (30). Beginning around 50°C, nesquehonite 335

begins to dehydrate with heating (31), releasing water into the system, and then the 336

structure begins to decompose around 100 °C (32). Hence, if the detected phase is similar 337

to nesquehonite (Fig. 3E), it is conceivable that it represents a persistent low-temperature 338

formation environment (19), where fluids were sufficiently alkaline (pH ~8.5–12.5) (33). 339

Amherst Point represents a chemically dynamic environment. The persistence of unaltered 340

Prolonged shallow subsurface preservation of hydrated carbonate 406

That metastable hydrated Mg-carbonate remains detectable in Martian shallow 407

subsurface settings is intriguing. The abrasion at Amherst Point reaches a depth of 408

approximately 1 cm (deeper than other abrasions), where the hydrated Mg-carbonate was 409

previously preserved in the subsurface. Thermal modeling and experimental constraints 410 indicate that Mars’s diurnal thermal skin depth, which defines how deeply the daily 411 temperature cycle penetrates the surface, is ~4-5 cm for typical regolith parameters (e.g., 412

grain size, porosity, and thermal inertia) (41-43). Thus, preservation of hydrated Mg- 413 carbonate even at 1 cm below the surface suggests that 1) daily temperature fluctuation 414 (44) is already significantly reduced or is almost negligible at this depth, 2) the Martian 415 regolith is an efficient thermal insulator even over 1.5 cm depth (43) to prevent mineral 416 dehydration, and 3) Martian shallow subsurface (1.5 cm) is frigid (mean temperature 417 ~-30 °C) (43), which can drastically reduce the rate of dehydration (see Supplementary 418 Text) (45 and references therein). 419

The kinetic factors of hydrated Mg-carbonate transformation under Mars surface or 420

shallow subsurface conditions are not well known, and therefore, modelling of the 421

formation and preservation is difficult at this time. Metastable hydrated carbonates like 422

lansfordite and nesquehonite are prone to dehydrating into dypingite or hydromagnesite 423

over timescales of days at ~50–60 °C (31). According to the Arrhenius equation (see 424

Supplementary Text), the low thermal energy exponentially suppresses reaction kinetics. 425

The activation energy for this transformation in the presence of silica is reported to 426

be ~64.9 kJ mol⁻¹ (26), and although it varies across studies (e.g., 46), we adopt this value 427

because abundant silica is also present in Amherst Point (see Fig. 5C and D). 428

Extrapolating this behavior to Martian shallow subsurface conditions (~–30 °C) (43) and 429

applying the Arrhenius relationship implies that such transformations would be 430

suppressed by several thousand times relative to laboratory conditions, extending 431

timescales from days to effectively geological time scales. If the detected hydrated 432

carbonate is similar to nesquehonite (Fig. 3E), it suggests that it did not fully transform 433

into dypingite or hydromagnesite (19) in those locations. Hence, the Martian shallow- 434

subsurface environment dramatically slows or effectively “freezes” the transformation 435

process. 436

Additionally, surface radiation appears to be mitigated entirely at shallow depths, 437 allowing for long-term stability of hydration. In a Mars simulation chamber experiment 438


<!-- Page 15 -->


(47), hydrated Mg-carbonate, such as hydromagnesite, was exposed to low pressures 439

(from 660 Pa to ~1 Pa), a CO₂-dominated atmosphere, UV radiation, and a temperature of 440

~25°C for more than 25 days. They observed no significant changes in water-related 441

absorption bands (in the near-infrared spectrum), indicating that the hydromagnesite had 442

not dehydrated. Although exposure to Martian surface conditions in the laboratory does 443

not fully replicate the billions of years of environmental exposure on Mars, SHERLOC 444

typically analyzes the freshly exposed surface of abraded rock approximately 36 hours 445

after the rover makes the abrasion (48). This brief exposure time suggests that the 446

hydrated Mg-carbonate at Amherst Point was likely not subjected to prolonged contact 447

(e.g., fewer than 25 days) with the Martian atmosphere, allowing it to remain stable and 448

detectable by the SHERLOC instrument. It is possible that even shallow subsurface 449

shielding likely contributed to maintaining the mineral's stability prior to abrasion (48). 450

Subsurface shielding of hydrated phases appears to be the most plausible explanation; 451

however, the current Mars atmosphere does not remove all water from minerals even on 452

the surface. SuperCam on board Perseverance sees hydration bands on natural surface 453

targets (48,49), but we do not know their initial hydration state (including 454

adsorbed/absorbed H2O) or how quickly they transform into other mineral phases. 455

SuperCam also often observes deeper H2O absorption bands in the infrared (1.9 µm) in 456

abrasions vs natural surface targets (25,49). However, SuperCam measures bulk 457

hydration in the infrared because the rocks are composed of multiple minerals (such as 458

phyllosilicates, sulfates, and carbonates) and the hydration cannot be confidently assigned 459

to a single phase. Therefore, SHERLOC’s high spatial resolution analyses, with a 100 µm 460

spot size (15), help identify phases that might otherwise be missed. In any case, water in 461

hydrated Mg-carbonate minerals is structurally bound within the crystal lattice, which 462

would have made it resistant to loss under Mars' surface or shallow subsurface conditions 463

(50). 464

The preservation of hydrated carbonate likely reflects a combination of textural and 465

geochemical stabilization processes. PIXL phase maps (Fig. 5, A and B) reveal hydrated 466

Mg-carbonate spatially associated with silica veins. Dissolved silica in aqueous media is 467

known to influence the interfacial stability of nesquehonite, lowering its nucleation 468

barrier and enhancing resistance to transformation into hydromagnesite (26). In addition 469

to silica, the fine-scale variability of coexisting hydrous and anhydrous magnesium 470

sulfates within a few hundred microns suggests that these phases may have contributed to 471

maintaining hydration in carbonates. Sulfate ions in natural brines can reduce the rate of 472

magnesite precipitation by promoting dissolution of hydrated Mg-carbonate and forming 473

strong MgSO₄ aqueous complexes, thereby limiting the availability of free Mg²⁺ (51). 474

Laboratory studies further indicate that coexisting phases can modulate the hydration– 475

dehydration kinetics of precipitated sulfates, favoring hydrated sulfate phases that are not 476

in thermodynamic equilibrium (52). Moreover, the transformation from nesquehonite to 477


<!-- Page 16 -->


hydromagnesite can be suppressed under Ca²⁺-poor, Mg²⁺-rich conditions (31, 51), even 478

under inert atmospheric conditions (pH₂O = pCO₂ = 10⁻⁴ mbar) at subzero temperatures 479

(53). This aligns with the PIXL-derived chemistry from Amherst Point and the inferred 480

restoration of a nesquehonite-like phase (Fig. 5 and Fig. S1). Micro-scale interactions 481

with hygroscopic perchlorate and phosphate-rich fluid may have also helped preserve 482

hydration in carbonates via micro-localized humidity modulation and protective surface 483

coatings (54-56). However, direct evidence for the role of these physicochemical 484

parameters in long-term preservation of hydration in carbonates on Mars is lacking and 485

warrants future experimental testing. 486

Overall, a spatially limited and localized presence of hydrated Mg-carbonates is expected 487

for such metastable minerals. Their long-term preservation, therefore, indicates 488

exceptional local boundary conditions of Amherst Point – specifically, water-rich, 489

alkaline chemistry combined with effective thermal and diagenetic shielding in the 490

shallow subsurface. A localized long-term preservation of metastable phases, thus, could 491

be a defining feature for Martian mineral discoveries that reflect environmental 492

heterogeneity rather than rarity of formation. As such, this occurrence provides a 493

uniquely sensitive record of ancient aqueous geochemistry and shallow subsurface 494

preservation aspects, strengthening its significance for understanding Mars’s CO₂ cycling 495

and unappreciated hydrated niches. 496

Hydrous phases and redox diversity as windows into early Jezero habitability 497

The presence of hydrated carbonate and sulfate implies that the local Jezero environment 498

was once CO₂-rich and contained liquid water, supporting the notion that the crater 499

hosted a warm and wet environment during the late Noachian (~4 to 3.7 Gya), a time 500

when early life was emerging on Earth (e.g., 57). Hydrated magnesium carbonates are 501

particularly diagnostic of alkaline conditions and indicate sustained water–rock 502

interaction in the presence of Mg and dissolved CO₂ (10). Laboratory studies show that 503

these hydrated phases preferentially form and persist under low-ionic-strength waters, 504

whereas magnesites are favored at higher salinities (51), highlighting a geochemical 505

context of their detection. Importantly, low ionic strength is also regarded as more 506

conducive to habitability (58). Taken together, newly discovered hydrated carbonate on 507

Mars suggests that this site may have preserved unusually low-salinity aqueous 508

environments, capable of sustaining liquid water even into the late Hesperian, when most 509

other regions of Mars had already dried (~3.6 Gya), although it became patchy and 510

discontinuous (59). 511

The coexistence of olivine and hydrous and anhydrous carbonates (Figs. 3A and B) 512

points to carbonation and serpentinization reactions, which not only buffer fluid 513

chemistry but also generate hydrogen and enhance redox gradients, widening the 514


<!-- Page 17 -->


potential window for habitable conditions on early Mars (60). This mineral assemblage 515

also indicates incomplete or episodic alteration, consistent with a multi-stage fluid 516

history. Hydrous carbonates are especially significant in this context, as their low- 517

temperature formation pathways are less destructive and more conducive to preserving 518

textural or chemical biosignatures (22). Silica and carbonates precipitated during 519

carbonation (22), as can be inferred from hydrated carbonates localized within silica 520

veins in Amherst Point (Fig. 5B), can preserve organics in low-temperature, water-rock 521

reaction conditions (61). However, co-occurrence of anhydrous carbonates likely reflects 522

later thermal maturation or dehydration, marking a shift from earlier clement conditions 523

to drier, less favorable environments. Together, these carbonate–silica vein and hydrous 524

and anhydrous mineral assemblages provide a mineralogical archive of evolving surface 525

and shallow-subsurface aqueous conditions. 526

The spatial association of sulfate, phosphate, and perchlorate alongside olivine, silica, 527

and both hydrous and anhydrous Mg-carbonates within the bedrock points to a 528

geochemical system containing both oxidants and reductants, nutrient sources, and 529

reservoirs of carbon – ingredients broadly consistent with the potential for diverse redox 530

and metabolic pathways. Sulfates represent a potential electron acceptor in microbial 531

redox metabolism, supporting processes such as sulfate reduction that are central to 532

anaerobic life, while phosphates are indispensable as structural components of nucleic 533

acids and energy carriers in biological systems (e.g., 62,63). Perchlorates, although 534

strongly oxidizing and capable of imposing oxidative stress on organics (64), can 535

paradoxically aid in their preservation under cold and dry conditions, and are also known 536

to serve as terminal electron acceptors for specialized microorganisms on Earth (e.g., 537

65,66). 538

However, the mere presence of such phases does not demonstrate that any such redox 539

reactions actually occurred; rather, it indicates that the chemical precursors necessary for 540

habitability (five out of six essential elements of life-as-we-know-it: Carbon, Hydrogen, 541

Nitrogen, Oxygen, Phosphorus, and Sulfur or CHNOPS) were present in this 542

microenvironment. In other words, the mineralogical associations captured at Amherst 543

Point represent a preserved record of the conditions that could have sustained 544

habitability, even if redox activity never took place. 545

Overall, water–rock reaction–driven carbonation would have been active locally under a 546

CO₂-rich atmosphere (5) when the ancient Jezero crater margin hosted warm, alkaline 547

waters long enough to form hydrated Mg-carbonate. The local Jezero environment could 548

have supported habitability during this interval in the late Noachian to early Hesperian 549

(~3.8–3.6 Ga). Thereafter, conditions likely shifted as Mars progressively lost CO₂ and 550

water potentially through carbonate formation post–3.5 Ga (6). Although this discovery 551

of hydrated Mg-carbonate alone cannot reconcile the missing-carbonate problem (6), it 552


<!-- Page 18 -->


provides a critical link between orbital detections and surface processes. Most 553

importantly, since then, the local shallow subsurface conditions within the Margin unit 554

may have remained stable, preserving the minerals’ hydration state. The preservation of 555

carbonate hydrate further indicates that the Amherst Point rock did not experience 556

elevated temperatures (due to metamorphism, hydrothermalism, or deep burial, etc.). 557

Rather, the hydrated carbonates represent relics of ancient fluid–rock interactions in a 558

shallow-subsurface environment. In any case, the discovery expands the surface 559

inventory of carbonate phases on Mars and offers new evidence of Mars’s long-missing 560

CO2 sink (6). 561

The Amherst Point abrasion target – an aqueously-deposited clastic rock containing 563

silica, phosphate, sulfate, and most importantly, carbonate minerals preserved in their 564

hydration states – provided the incentive to acquire the first rock core sample of the 565

Margin unit named “Pelican Point” (Fig. 1F) (Sample 22, drilled on sol 923) (67) for 566
